doc.title: Kristen Korb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000

title: Finding jazz in Montana and college in Billings
summary: Gene Harris missed in Boise; record clubs with her brothers; Eastern Montana College festival and Emily Remler's advice to take lessons; moving to San Diego to study with Turetzky.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Well there’s more jazz in Idaho than there is in Montana?

Well at least I thought there was. I mean I think it’s all over but it’s just where you look. And I think as long as you’re open to it and receptive to it, it will find you. And it was one of those things that even though I was living in Boise, Idaho at the time when Gene Harris was there, because of my age and the society there, it was not cool for a seventh or an eighth grader to go to the local bar to go hear jazz musicians. So I never actually got to know who Gene Harris was until after I’d moved away. But when I got to Montana, in high school and everything, I ran into people — oh you like jazz, oh, here listen to this, here, check this out. And so making tapes for friends and going back and forth, and my brothers got into the music so they started signing up for every record club, Columbia House and BMG Jazz Club, and played drop the needle tests with me at three o’clock in the morning, and come jumping into my bed. And it was one of those things that even though Montana was not the place necessarily for jazz, I did find it, and people that love the music, and that were encouraging. And then when I was in college I went to Eastern Montana College in Billings. And I started my own groups, played in the jazz band, and we had a jazz festival that I became student director of, and we had like Maynard Ferguson and George Shearing came and we had some people from California come in, some professors, John Prince, guitarist Tom Bevan came in, Bobby Shew was there. And so through meeting these people and just hanging out with everybody that I could, Emily Remler, the great guitar player, came through Billings about four months before she died, so I got to hang with her a little bit. She said some really important things. She said get lessons from whoever you can. When you go to a town, you study with the people that are there. If somebody comes to your town, you get a lesson with them. It doesn’t have to be anything more than a lesson but you need to hang with these people if this is what you want to do. So I got my bachelor’s in Music Ed, moved down to San Diego to study bass with Bert Turetzky at UCSD, and then Ray Brown came through San Diego. And the first year I was just like oh it’s Ray Brown, oh I want a lesson, I want a lesson. And I went up to him and shook his hand and I’m like, “Oh Mr. Brown, I really enjoyed your performance,” and he was in one of those moods, you know he was kind of like the king welcoming the court at the end of the gig. And he didn’t say anything, not hello, good
